entities.name: Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Seated Woman of Çatalhöyük, a Neolithic figurine discovered at the archaeological site of Çatalhöyük in modern-day Turkey, dates back to approximately 6000 BCE. This artifact is significant as it embodies the artistic and cultural expressions of early agricultural societies and provides insight into the socio-religious dynamics of prehistoric communities. Unearthed during the 1960s by British archaeologist James Melaart, this figurine has captured the attention of historians and archaeologists, symbolizing the connection between gender roles and ritual practices in early human civilizations.

The Seated Woman is a stylized representation of a female figure, often interpreted as a fertility symbol or a representation of a mother goddess. This interpretation is supported by the presence of similar figurines found across various sites in the Near East, suggesting a shared cultural motif among Neolithic peoples. The discovery of the sculpture in the context of a densely populated settlement reveals much about the social structure of Çatalhöyük, where communal living and the practice of agriculture transformed human lifestyles and economic practices around 7000 years ago.

The legacy of the Seated Woman extends beyond its immediate physical presence. It has become a focal point for discussions about the role of women in early societies and the significance of figurative art in expressing communal beliefs. The figurine has influenced contemporary interpretations of prehistoric culture, prompting scholars to reevaluate the narratives surrounding gender and societal structure in early agricultural communities. Moreover, it has inspired modern artistic expressions and continues to be an emblem of female representation in archaeology.
